questions.prompt: What unit is used to measure the mass of atoms?
questions.explanation: Atomic mass is measured in atomic mass units (amu), where one amu is about the mass of a single proton or neutron.
questions.misconception: Atoms are far too small to weigh in everyday units like kilograms — the atomic mass unit is a special scale just for particles this tiny.

questions.prompt: What makes up nearly all of an atom's mass?
questions.explanation: Protons and neutrons each weigh about 1 amu and make up nearly all of an atom's mass. Electrons are far too light to matter here.
questions.misconception: Electrons are the famous moving particles, but they weigh about 1/1836 of a proton — nearly all the mass sits in the protons and neutrons.

questions.prompt: Why is carbon's atomic mass 12.011 instead of exactly 12?
options: It is a weighted average of carbon's isotopes
Carbon atoms are broken and lose mass
Carbon has extra electrons that add weight
questions.explanation: Carbon's atomic mass is a weighted average of all its naturally occurring isotopes — mostly carbon-12 with small amounts of heavier carbon-13 and -14.
questions.misconception: Atoms never lose or gain mass in chemistry, and electrons are far too light to shift a mass number — the decimal comes purely from mixing isotopes.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly tells the two numbers apart?
options: Atomic number names the element; atomic mass describes average weight
Atomic mass names the element; atomic number describes weight
They are two names for the same number
questions.explanation: The atomic number is the proton count that identifies the element; the atomic mass is the average weight of its atoms including neutrons.
questions.misconception: They sound similar and sit side by side on the card, but they measure different things — identity versus weight — and never match.
